question: I want to do issue 42 myself. How do I stop the bot picking it up in the meantime, and how do I give it back to the bot later?
answer: Assign the issue to someone, for example yourself: assignment is the reservation switch, and the pipeline's issue gatherer drops every assigned issue before the selecting model is shown its candidates, so a reserved issue is never considered at all. Unassign it to give it back; the assignee is part of what the pipeline watches for changes, so the next cycle sees the issue again. Setting its Priority to Low is not a reservation, because a Low issue is still selected once nothing above it is waiting. A `blocked` label also keeps an issue out, but it tells readers the work is waiting on something rather than that someone has claimed it.
must_mention: assign the issue (assignment is the reservation)
assigned issues are dropped before selection and never considered
unassigning releases it and the next cycle picks it up again
a Low priority does not keep an issue out of the pipeline

question: Issue 42 can't be started until issue 41 is merged. How do I make the bot wait for 41, and will I have to remember to undo that afterwards?
answer: Put `Blocked-by: #41` on its own line in issue 42's body or in any comment on it; for an item in another repository the pipeline works, write it in full as `Blocked-by: owner/repo#41`, and several references can share one line separated by commas or spaces. Every cycle the pipeline checks the referenced item's live open or closed state in code, not by a model's reading, and keeps 42 out of its candidates while 41 is open. As soon as every referenced item is closed (closing or merging it is enough), 42 becomes selectable again, and if it had been recorded as blocked that block clears automatically, logged as `dependency-resolved`. You need not edit or remove the line afterwards: a `Blocked-by:` line naming a closed item is simply inert.
must_mention: a `Blocked-by: #41` line on its own line in the issue body or a comment
the `owner/repo#41` form for an item in another repository
released automatically once the referenced item closes
the line need not be removed afterwards

question: Some of my issues now have a 'refined' label (pw::refined) and a long comment from the bot listing goals and acceptance criteria. What does that mean, and does it matter if I take the label off?
answer: It means the pipeline's Refiner, a cheap model run at the end of a cycle, has written the issue a specification (the goal, what is in and out of scope, and concrete acceptance criteria) as one comment on the issue, and that comment is part of the thread the work is done from when the issue is selected. Under the default refinement policy for issues (`preferred`), a refined issue is ranked ahead of an otherwise equal unrefined one, although an unrefined issue can still be picked. The label (`refined_label`, `pw::refined` by default) is purely informational: nothing reads it back, so removing it by hand changes nothing, because the pipeline's own log is the record. If the specification later proves inadequate and the issue is flagged as needing refinement, the pipeline takes the refined label off itself.

question: I opened a pull request myself, it now has merge conflicts, and I haven't time to finish it. Can I hand it over to the bot, and what do I have to do?
answer: Yes: add the label the pipeline puts on every pull request it raises (the `pr_label` setting, `autonomous-agent` in the README's examples), and the next cycle treats the pull request as work, rebasing a ready one that has hit a merge conflict and resolving the conflict, finishing a stalled draft, or answering changes you have requested. It only works for a branch under the pipeline's branch prefix (`agent/` in the README's examples), so put the work on a branch named like `agent/<something>` first; a labelled pull request on any other branch is ignored. Labelling gives the pipeline write access to the branch, including a `--force-with-lease` rebase, and you take the pull request back by removing the label.

the label lets the pipeline push to the branch, including a force-pushed rebase

question: How do I get the bot to do a particular issue sooner, and will the issues nobody has got round to triaging just sit there for ever?
answer: Set the issue's `Priority` field, GitHub's own issue field (Urgent, High, Medium or Low) set from the issue sidebar, not a label. `Urgent` puts the issue second overall across every configured repository, behind only security alerts and ahead even of answering review feedback, while `High`, `Medium` and `Low` place it progressively lower within its repository's ordering, with `Low` above only the automated code-quality findings. An issue with no Priority set counts as `Medium`, exactly where issues ranked before priorities existed, so untriaged issues are still picked up, and no band, not even `Low`, keeps an issue out. Priority does not override the exclusions: an assigned, `blocked`-labelled or `Blocked-by:`-held issue stays out even when `Urgent`, and a change of priority is noticed on the next cycle.
must_mention: the `Priority` issue field, not a label
Urgent is second only to security, across all repositories
an issue with no Priority set counts as Medium
Priority does not override exclusions such as assignment or the blocked label

question: I asked for changes on one of the bot's pull requests. What will it do with my review, and what do I need to do to get the pull request merged after that?
answer: The next cycle picks the review up ahead of new work (only security alerts and `Urgent` issues outrank answering review feedback) and passes every review body and inline comment in that round to the agent verbatim. It pushes its fixes to the same branch, never opening a second pull request or redoing the original work, replies point by point saying what it changed, what it did not and why, and re-requests your review, checking with GitHub that the re-request actually happened. It never dismisses your review, so your `CHANGES_REQUESTED` keeps the pull request blocked until you re-review it yourself, at every merge-autonomy level. If only some of your findings should block the merge, say which; the agent honours that split.
must_mention: fixes are pushed to the same branch and pull request, not a new one
it replies point by point and re-requests your review
your changes-requested review keeps it blocked until you re-review; the pipeline never dismisses it
only security work and Urgent issues are picked ahead of answering review feedback

question: The bot closed one of my issues saying the work was already done, but it isn't. I reopened the issue and nothing happened. How do I get the bot to take it on again?
answer: The pipeline recorded that item as void (no work to do), a verdict no agent can ever clear, and while that verdict is still being carried a plain reopen of the closed issue changes nothing. Apply the unvoid label (`unvoid_label`, `pw::unvoided` by default and `unvoided` in the README's examples) to that issue, or to any issue or pull request in the same repository that names the item; the next cycle reopens the void and the item is back among the candidates in that same cycle. No pipeline stage ever applies this label, so only a human can do this, and you should leave the label in place: it only reopens voids recorded before you applied it, so it can never quietly cancel a later verdict. Once a void has retired (its issue closed and the void older than `void_retire_after_days`, 30 days by default), reopening the issue alone is enough.

question: The bot left one of its own draft pull requests half-finished. Will it come back and finish it, and what should I do if I don't want that draft at all?
answer: Yes: a draft the pipeline raised that has had no real activity (a push, a review or a comment, not label edits or the pipeline's own comments) for longer than `abandoned_draft_after_hours`, by default derived from the schedule to span four cycle firings, becomes an abandoned-draft work item, and the pipeline finishes it on the existing branch and pull request rather than starting over. It ranks ahead of fresh work, after only security alerts, Urgent issues, review feedback, merge conflicts and pull requests a merge queue dropped. If you do not want the draft, label the pull request `obsolete`: at the default settings the pipeline will not close a draft that still changes files on its own judgement (it escalates to you instead), but the next time it records the item as void the label corroborates that verdict and the pull request is closed with a comment naming the label. Only a human applies `obsolete`; no pipeline stage ever does.

question: How can I tell from GitHub whether the bot has already started on one of my issues, and which comments on it are the bot's rather than a person's?
answer: When the pipeline starts on an issue it immediately opens a draft pull request, labelled with its pull-request label and stating the item and the planned approach, on a branch named for the item under its branch prefix (for example `agent/<item>`), and comments on the issue linking that draft, so a linked draft from the pipeline means the work is claimed and in progress. The pull request stays a draft until the Reviewer stage has checked it and marked it ready for review, which is when it reaches your review queue. Every comment the pipeline posts opens with a bold line naming the stage that wrote it and the node that ran it, such as **Implementer** · autonomous pipeline · node `<node>`, because its comments can appear under the same GitHub account a person uses; a comment without that line was written by a human.
must_mention: it opens a draft pull request carrying its label as soon as it starts
it comments on the issue linking that draft pull request
every pipeline comment opens with a bold line naming the stage and the node
a comment without that line was written by a human

question: I'm about to roll out a risky change and want the whole fleet to stop working for a while: no new work, and no more work on the pull requests it already has open. I don't want to kill anything that is running at this moment, though. What do I run, and how long will the pause last?
answer: From any one node, run `docker compose exec scheduler /app/agent-cycle.sh --disable "<reason>"` (a reason is required); it also publishes a fleet-wide flag that every node checks at the start of its next cycle, so the whole fleet stands down. It stops the next cycle, not one already running: a cycle in flight finishes, `--status` shows whether one is running, and you should not run `docker compose up -d`, `restart` or `down` by hand until it reads idle, because that kills the running cycle (watchtower's rolls wait by themselves). Unless you pass `--for` (for example `8h` or `forever`) or `--until`, the pause expires after `disable_default_ttl`, which by default is derived as four cycle firings, one hour at the default 15-minute cadence. `--enable` from any node lifts it everywhere.
must_mention: `agent-cycle.sh --disable` with a reason, run on any one node, stops every node
a cycle already running is allowed to finish; only the next cycle is stopped
do not recreate or restart the containers by hand until `--status` shows the node idle
it expires after four cycle firings (an hour at the default cadence) unless `--for` or `--until` is given, and `--enable` resumes

question: My node fires every quarter of an hour, but all morning its log shows each run giving up without doing anything. How do I see why, and is something broken?
answer: Every run that gives up logs a `stand-down` event with a `reason` in the node's cycle log (`log.jsonl` in the state directory); `./watch-node.sh events` from the stack directory shows it, or you can filter the log with `jq 'select(.event == "stand-down")'`. A reason beginning `no-op short-circuit` is the system working as designed: nothing the work-selection step reads has changed since it last found nothing to do, so the run skips the paid model call. Selection is forced to run regardless once the last nothing-to-do verdict is `none_selected_recheck_hours` old (by default derived as 24 firings, six hours at the default 15-minute cadence), and `agent-cycle.sh --once` forces it immediately. If `--once` then picks up work the scheduled runs were skipping, the fingerprint is missing a signal, which is a bug worth filing.
must_mention: each skipped run logs a `stand-down` event with a reason in the cycle log (`log.jsonl`), viewable with `watch-node.sh events`
a reason beginning `no-op short-circuit` means nothing has changed since the last nothing-to-do verdict, which is normal
selection is forced anyway after `none_selected_recheck_hours` (24 firings, six hours at the default cadence)
`agent-cycle.sh --once` bypasses the skip immediately

question: One of my nodes needs to reach a preview site on our own custom domain, and its requests are being refused. How do I let that node through without opening it up on every node?
answer: A node's pipeline container reaches the internet only through the egress proxy's domain allowlist, which permits HTTPS to the listed domains and refuses everything else. To add a domain for one node, put it in that node's `.env` as `EGRESS_EXTRA_ALLOW=preview.example.com` (comma- or whitespace-separated for several) and run `docker compose up -d egress-proxy`. A domain every node needs belongs instead in `deploy/docker/egress-allowlist.txt`, changed through a pull request, where `test/egress-fence.test.sh` pins the set. If everything times out rather than only that domain, check `DOCKER_MTU` first; the Egress section of `scripts/doctor.sh` tells the failure shapes apart.
must_mention: add the domain to `EGRESS_EXTRA_ALLOW` in that node's `.env`
apply it with `docker compose up -d egress-proxy`

question: We're getting rid of one of our machines for good. How do I take its node out so that nothing of it is left behind?
answer: First check with `--status` that at least one other node is active, because the fleet elects no replacement and removing the last active node silently stops all work, and let any running cycle finish, using `--disable '<reason>' --this-node` so the node starts no new one. Then, from its stack directory, log its Tailscale sidecar out if it has one and run `docker compose down -v --remove-orphans`, so its volumes are destroyed along with its containers. Only after the stack is down, delete its `nodes/<NODE_NAME>` branch from the state repository (a node still running would push it back within five minutes); every peer then prunes it, and its dashboard card, at its next fetch. Finally revoke the node's GitHub token (and any dedicated Tailscale key) rather than merely deleting `.env`, then delete the stack directory and reclaim the image disk.
must_mention: confirm that at least one other node is active before removing it
`docker compose down -v` so the volumes are removed too
delete its `nodes/<NODE_NAME>` branch from the state repository, and only after the stack is down
revoke the node's GitHub token rather than just deleting `.env`

question: I've just brought up a new node. Is there a single check that tells me whether the whole installation is set up correctly before I let it start working?
answer: Run `docker compose exec scheduler /app/scripts/doctor.sh`, inside the container, because that is where the toolchain and credentials are. It checks `config.json` against the schema, the model ids, prompts, toolchain, writable directories, the rendered crontab, the GitHub access the token really has (including whether it can push) and whether `claude` is logged in, giving each check `ok`, `warn`, `fail` or `skip`; any `fail` makes it exit 1. It is safe on a live node, even mid-cycle, because every GitHub call it makes is a read and it writes only a few declared things; `--offline` limits it to the configuration, toolchain and crontab. Every node also runs `doctor.sh --unattended` by itself once an hour, and that pass's warnings and failures appear in the Doctor section of the dashboard.
must_mention: `scripts/doctor.sh`, run inside the scheduler container
each check reads `ok`, `warn`, `fail` or `skip`, and a `fail` exits non-zero

an hourly unattended pass reports to the dashboard's Doctor section

question: I need to do maintenance on one machine for a couple of hours while the other nodes keep working. How do I stop just that one, and how do I bring it back?
answer: On that node run `docker compose exec scheduler /app/agent-cycle.sh --disable "<reason>" --this-node --for 2h`, and `--enable --this-node` when you are done. `--this-node` writes only that node's own switch record and never touches the fleet-wide flag, so the rest of the fleet keeps working; a plain `--disable` without it would stop every node. It needs no container recreate or role change, shows on that node's `--status` and dashboard card, and expires on the same terms as the fleet switch (`disable_default_ttl` unless `--for` or `--until` says otherwise), so a forgotten enable costs only a few cycles. To stop the node spending indefinitely instead, set `ROLE=standby` in its `.env` and run `docker compose up -d`.

question: I merged a fix to the pipeline's code a while ago, but one node still shows the old version on the dashboard. How does a new version reach the nodes, and when should I start worrying?
answer: A merge to `main` that touches anything the container reads makes CI publish a new image as `ghcr.io/pullwright/agent-ops:latest`, and on nodes running the `auto-update` profile watchtower pulls it on its roughly five-minute poll and restarts the services into it; a documentation-only merge publishes no image at all. A roll never interrupts a cycle: watchtower's pre-update hook exits 75 while either pipeline's lock is held, so the update slides to the next poll until the node is idle, and a node reading behind for a while is normal. The dashboard's fleet strip shows a grey `image behind` badge until the newest image is older than `image_behind_grace_hours` (3 hours by default), and an amber one after that. At that point check `docker compose logs watchtower` to see whether it is still polling, and run `./check-node-image.sh` from the stack directory for a live check against the registry.

question: We ran into our Claude usage limit, so I've raised the spending cap, but running --enable didn't get the nodes going again. What actually brings them back?
answer: A usage-limit stand-down is a separate state from the on/off switch, so `--enable` does not touch it; `--status` reports it on its own `limit:` line. Once the cap is really raised, run `docker compose exec scheduler /app/agent-cycle.sh --clear-limit "cap raised"` on any node: it deletes the `fleet/limit.json` flag in the state repository and logs a `limit-cleared` event, which the other nodes pick up at their next state-sync fetch. Left alone, a stand-down whose message stated no reset time lifts by itself, because each cycle probes the account with one minimal request and retires the stand-down the moment the account answers; one with a stated reset time simply waits until then. Clear it only when the limit is actually gone, or the next cycle hits it again and stands the fleet down afresh.
must_mention: `--enable` does not lift a usage-limit stand-down
`agent-cycle.sh --clear-limit` lifts it for the whole fleet

question: None of my nodes has opened a pull request in days, and nothing looks obviously wrong. Where should I look first?
answer: Start with `docker compose exec scheduler /app/agent-cycle.sh --status`, because a pipeline someone switched off looks exactly like a quiet week, and `--status` shows both the on/off switch (cleared with `--enable`) and any usage-limit stand-down. If the switch is on, read the cron log (`./watch-node.sh cron`): a line reading `skipped — this node is standby` means that node does not spend, and one saying the value `is not a role` is a misspelling standing it down. Only the exact value `active` makes a node work (unset, empty or misspelt all mean standby), so set `ROLE=active` in the `.env` of each node that should work, as many as you like, and run `docker compose up -d`.

question: What would I actually have to provide to get one instance of this running on my own infrastructure: what kind of machine, which accounts and which keys?
answer: A host with Docker and nothing else installed: the image carries the whole toolchain, is published for both linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, and a 2-core VM with 20 GB of disk is comfortable because the workspaces hold full clones. A GitHub token for the node with read and write access to every repository it works on (contents, pull requests, issues, workflows and actions) plus read access to security alerts, one token per node so that a single node can be revoked. A git identity, a name and an email, for the commits the node makes; an active node's cycles refuse to run without both. Model credentials: an Anthropic API key (the primary path, shareable by any number of nodes) or a Claude subscription logged in interactively once per node; a Tailscale pre-auth key is needed only if you want the dashboard on your tailnet rather than on the machine's own loopback.

question: Which of its pull requests, if any, will it merge into my repositories without a person signing off?
answer: Out of the box, none: `merge_autonomy` defaults to `human`, so a person approves and merges every pull request, and it stays there until you deliberately raise it for one repository or for the whole installation. At `agent-merges-routine` it lands a pull request itself only when its complexity grade is in `merge_autonomy_routine_complexity` (`low` and `medium` by default), its work source is in `merge_autonomy_routine_sources` (only `tech-debt` by default) and it touches no protected path (by default the gate code, prompts, CI and configuration paths such as `.github/*`), and only after the required checks are green, the security-alert delta is clean and an independent Approver review has approved it. `agent-merges-all` additionally lands a pull request that touches a protected path, but only after a critical-tier Approver review and a `landing_cool_off_hours` wait (24 hours by default) that restarts if anything is pushed after the approval. Even at that top level, a pull request the merge queue has ever removed without merging, one whose latest round answered a `landing-refusals` comment, and one whose source cannot be read back from the log still need your click.

question: If I point this at a private codebase, where do my code and my issue text end up? What actually leaves the machine it runs on?
answer: The container that runs the agents can reach the internet only through an egress proxy with a domain allowlist (GitHub, the Anthropic API, Vercel previews, the npm registry and its build-time font hosts, and the image registry), and Claude Code's optional traffic (updates, telemetry and error reporting) is switched off at source. So what a stage reads from your repositories goes to Anthropic as model input, and what it produces goes back to GitHub as branches, pull requests and comments. If you configure a state repository so that several nodes can share their memory, each node also pushes its event log, cycle records and cron logs to that private GitHub repository, after redacting home paths and anything token-shaped. The dashboard is never exposed to a network: it is served only to your own tailnet or to the machine's loopback.

Claude Code telemetry, updates and error reporting are switched off

question: What am I going to be paying for in model usage? Which part is the expensive part, and does it still cost money when there is nothing to do?
answer: You pay for model usage directly, through your own Anthropic API key (the primary path) or your Claude subscription. With the model choices the documented cost profile assumes, a working cycle's dominant cost is its one implementation pass (Sonnet), alongside a small Haiku selection pass and one review (Sonnet, or Opus only for work graded `complexity:high`). When nothing the selector reads has changed, a firing skips the model call entirely and costs only a few GitHub calls, and a standby node spends nothing at all. The expensive optional stages are bounded too: the merge Approver is never engaged at the default `merge_autonomy` of `human`, and the stage that re-examines blocked items, if you enable it, looks at a permanently stuck item at most once every 72 hours by default. The dashboard shows estimated token cost by day, by model and by actor.

question: Can I use it with a code host other than GitHub, such as GitLab, or with models from a provider other than Anthropic?
answer: Not today. GitHub is the only supported forge: it is reached through `gh` and GitHub-specific concepts (issues, labels, pull requests, checks, merge queues, App installations), and a forge-abstraction layer for others such as GitLab, Bitbucket or Gitea is intended but post-MVP, to be revisited on design-partner demand and built no earlier than after the Phase 4 launch. Anthropic is the only executable model provider: every model key takes a bare Claude model id or an `anthropic/`-qualified one, and a qualifier naming any other provider is rejected at cycle start with an error naming the key. Non-Claude providers are settled on the roadmap (D12, D29): xAI's Grok, run through its own Grok Build CLI, was brought forward into Phase 1 for a prospective customer and is being built, and further providers follow by design-partner demand in Phase 3.

question: If its judgement goes wrong, what stops it opening a flood of pull requests, or merging dozens of changes in a single day?
answer: Opening is capped by back-pressure: once its own draft pull requests, ready ones still under a `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review and its in-flight claims together reach `max_open_agent_prs` (a required setting), it starts no new work and only finishes pull requests already open (answering review feedback, fixing merge conflicts, completing abandoned drafts), standing down when there is nothing left to finish. Merging is capped by `merge_budget_per_day` (8 by default), a limit on how many pull requests it may land in one repository in any rolling 24 hours, counted from GitHub's own merged-pull-request record rather than a private counter. At the cap a pull request is still approved but not merged, so the backlog queues visibly. Landing more than the cap is treated as a counting anomaly: it freezes that repository to approval-only and files an escalation issue for a human.

question: If I run it on two machines for redundancy, what stops both of them picking up the same issue and doing the work twice?
answer: Before any work starts, the script (never the model) takes an atomic, create-only claim on the item, so GitHub itself arbitrates the race. For a new item the claim is the creation of its working branch, `agent/<item-ref>`, on the target repository; for finishing an existing pull request it is the creation of a claim file in the shared private state repository. If the create fails because the branch or file already exists, a peer holds the item, so the node logs `claim-lost` and moves on to its next-ranked candidate. There is no leader and no lease: any number of nodes may be active, per-node minute offsets keep them from firing at the same moment, and the shared log they all read is only an advisory speed-up on top of the claims.

question: Which GitHub identity approves and merges its pull requests? Could the same account that wrote the code simply wave it through?
answer: No. The pipeline authors every pull request with the node's own GitHub credential, and GitHub refuses to let a pull request's author approve it, so every merge level above `human` needs a second, non-author identity: the Pullwright Approver GitHub App. Its installation must hold exactly `contents: write`, `metadata: read` and `pull_requests: write` (`scripts/doctor.sh` fails anything else), and its installation token lives for about an hour. Only the deterministic script signs reviews and merges with that token, and only once every gate and an independent Approver verdict have passed; no model, not even the Approver stage's own prompt, ever holds approve or merge rights. The optional authoring App that can replace a node's personal access token is deliberately a different App, so the authoring identity can never approve its own work.

question: If I let it merge on its own and it starts doing something I do not like, how do I keep a veto over a single pull request, and how do I stop the automatic merging, or everything, at once?
answer: A `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review from your own GitHub account blocks landing at every autonomy level, unconditionally: the pipeline never dismisses a human review, so raising the level narrows what needs your merge click, never what needs your veto. To stop all automatic approval and merging at once, run `agent-cycle.sh --kill-merge-autonomy "<reason>"`: it forces every repository's effective level to `human` immediately and fleet-wide without editing `config.json`, while cycles carry on, until `agent-cycle.sh --restore-merge-autonomy` clears it. To stop the pipeline starting anything at all, `agent-cycle.sh --disable "<reason>"` stands the whole fleet down from the next cycle; it expires after `disable_default_ttl` unless you pass `--for forever`, and `--enable` resumes it.
must_mention: a CHANGES_REQUESTED review from your own account blocks landing at every level
--kill-merge-autonomy forces every repository back to human approval and merging fleet-wide without editing config.json

--disable stands the whole fleet down

question: I only want to run the tests for the part I changed, and against an image I have built from my own branch rather than the published one. How do I do that?
answer: Pass one or more name fragments to `./scripts/run-tests.sh` (for example `./scripts/run-tests.sh cycle-state doctor`) and it runs only the `test/*.test.sh` files whose names contain one of them; `--list` prints that selection without needing Docker. The script copies your working tree into a throwaway container built from the image, which by default is the latest one published on ghcr.io. To test against your own build instead, run `docker build -f deploy/docker/Dockerfile -t agent-ops:dev .` and then `AGENT_OPS_TEST_IMAGE=agent-ops:dev ./scripts/run-tests.sh`.

question: If I change how the pipeline behaves (say, how it chooses the next issue to work on), which documentation has to change with it, and should I update the spec or the prompt files first?
answer: The as-built specification for that component must change in the same pull request as the code: `docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PIPELINE-SPEC.md` for `agent-cycle.sh`, `lib/`, `scripts/` and the stage prompts, and `docs/REVIEW-PIPELINE-SPEC.md`, `docs/MONITOR-PIPELINE-SPEC.md` or `docs/DASHBOARD-SPEC.md` for the review pipeline, the Pipeline Monitor or the dashboard. Update the affected numbered requirement and any acceptance check anchored to it, or add a new requirement for new behaviour, stating only what is; history and rationale belong in the specification's design-decision and gotcha sections. The specifications outrank `prompts/*.md`, which implement them, so bring the specification in line first and then the affected prompts.

question: I am adding a new setting to config.schema.json for a feature. Apart from the code that reads it, what else does my pull request have to change or run before CI will accept it?
answer: The configuration tables in `README.md` and the specifications are generated from the schema, so document the key in the schema itself (its `description`, its `x-docs.readme` and `x-docs.spec` notes and, if needed, its `x-docs.value` cell) and never hand-edit a table row. Then run `scripts/render-config-table.sh` with no arguments to regenerate all four table regions (the README's two and the implementation and review specifications' own), and `scripts/render-config-table.sh --check` before pushing, because the config-table workflow runs that check on every pull request. The key's fallback value belongs in the schema's `default`, which readers pick up through `lib/config-schema.sh`'s `config_defaults` merge rather than a `// literal` of their own. The schema may use only the JSON Schema keywords `lib/config-schema.sh` implements (which `test/config-schema.test.sh` asserts), and the owning specification's requirement is updated in the same pull request as for any behaviour change.

question: The test I am writing depends on a configured threshold. Can I just read the number out of config.json, or assert what the shipped config sets it to?
answer: No. A test may assert only that the shipped `config.json` is valid (that it matches `config.schema.json` and that `scripts/doctor.sh` accepts it), never what values it holds. Each test supplies its own configuration, either by mutating `test/fixtures/config-base.json` or by writing its own block, and a check that genuinely concerns the shipped file reads the values back through `config_defaults`, the same resolution the code uses, rather than repeating them. The rule exists so that a routine configuration change (a threshold, a cadence, an autonomy level, a repository added or removed) never obliges anyone to edit a test.

question: My branch only edits one of the prompt files, which is just Markdown. Will merging it build a new image and roll it out to the nodes, and how can I check before I push?
answer: Yes. Only a short allowlist of prose paths counts as documentation-only (`docs/`, `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `TECH-DEBT.md`, `LICENCE` and `deploy/docker/README.md`), and everything else builds an image, `prompts/*.md` emphatically included, because those files are the instructions the pipeline feeds to `claude`. You can ask the classifier CI uses by running `git diff --no-renames --name-only main...HEAD | ./scripts/is-docs-only.sh`, which exits 0 only for a documentation-only change and otherwise prints the paths that force a build. Once such a change merges to `main`, the new image is published and every node on the `auto-update` profile restarts into it within watchtower's poll interval of about five minutes, waiting for any running cycle to finish first.

question: I am knowingly leaving a shortcut in my pull request to fix properly later. Where do I write that down, and how should the pull request refer to it?
answer: Record it as a GitHub issue labelled `pw::type:tech-debt`, not as a file under `tech-debt/` (a frozen archive) and not only in a commit message or chat. Search for an existing one first (`gh issue list --label pw::type:tech-debt --search "<working title>"`) and cite it rather than filing a duplicate. Put the shortcut and its provenance in the issue body (for example "Noticed while working #631"), then add a `Defers: #<n>` line to your pull request, never a closing keyword, because deferring is not resolving.

question: I am opening a fix: pull request against agent-ops. What has to be in its description for the checks to pass, and should I also add a line to CHANGELOG.md?
answer: Because the title's type is `fix` (the same holds for `feat`, `perf` and any type carrying the `!` breaking-change marker), the description must carry a `## Changelog` section: one or more of Keep a Changelog's category sub-headings (`### Added`, `### Changed`, `### Deprecated`, `### Removed`, `### Fixed`, `### Security`), each followed by `- ` bullets, or the single line `None.` for a change that is not notable; the changelog-section check fails the pull request otherwise. Do not edit `CHANGELOG.md`: the squash merge writes the description onto `main`, and only the release or scheduled-roll pull request assembles the file from those entries. If your head branch is named `agent/<n>`, CI also treats the pull request as issue-sourced and requires both the `<!-- agent-ops:closes-issue item=<n> -->` marker and a real closing keyword such as `Closes #<n>` in the body.

question: shellcheck is clean on my laptop, but the shell-lint check fails on my pull request. What is CI doing differently, and how do I reproduce it before pushing?
answer: CI installs a pinned shellcheck, v0.10.0, and runs `./scripts/lint-shell.sh`, which owns the file set (every tracked `*.sh` plus every file with a sh or bash shebang) and lints each file in its own process with `-x`; a developer host commonly has an older shellcheck such as 0.8.0, which misses findings CI fails on (SC2317, for one). Reproduce it by running `./scripts/lint-shell.sh` inside a container from the image, which installs the same pinned release. On a machine short of memory the script may lint the largest scripts without `-x`, or skip them, and says so on stderr, whereas CI sets `LINT_SHELL_FOLLOW_MIB` to 0 and checks every file in full. Clean means nothing reported, info findings included, and a false positive is silenced by a `# shellcheck disable=` comment with a reason in the file itself, never by an exclusion in the runner.

question: Before my branch merges, I would like to watch it run a real cycle on an actual node. How do I do that without putting the machines that do the real work at risk?
answer: Build the image from your checkout (`docker build -f deploy/docker/Dockerfile -t agent-ops .`), set `AGENT_OPS_IMAGE=agent-ops` in the stack's `.env`, and bring it up with `docker compose up -d`; then run `docker compose exec scheduler /app/agent-cycle.sh --dry-run`, or `--once --repo <repo>` for a single real cycle. Do this on a scratch stack or a standby node, never on the node doing the fleet's main work; `--dry-run` and `--once` run regardless of the node's role, so the test node can stay `standby` throughout. A second stack on the same host needs its own `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME`, node name and token.

question: Which requirement governs when a claim expires and is swept, how is the default expiry derived, and which test proves it?
answer: Requirement 17a governs it: claim-registry entries older than `claim_ttl_hours` are swept by `lib/claim.sh gc` under the only-if-untouched rule (a claim branch is deleted only if it still points at the recorded SHA and no open PR uses it), and because every cycle runs the sweep at start, a dead node's claims outlive it by at most the TTL plus one cycle interval. The default is not a fixed number of hours: requirement 1d derives `claim_ttl_hours` as 6 cadence firings of the worst-case gap between cycles, additionally floored at requirement 4f's stage-backstop quantity (`stage_budget_lock_seconds`), and a configured value acts as a floor under that derivation, never a ceiling. The proof is `test/claim.test.sh` (the unit test of `lib/claim.sh`, component 3e), whose `claims` section is acceptance check 7c: an entry older than `claim_ttl_hours` no longer appears among the visible claims.
must_mention: requirement 17a
entries older than claim_ttl_hours are swept by lib/claim.sh gc, which deletes a claim branch only if it is untouched and PR-less
requirement 1d derives the default as 6 firings of the worst-case gap between cycles, floored at the stage-backstop runtime
test/claim.test.sh (acceptance check 7c)

question: Which acceptance checks cover the landing cool-off for protected-path pull requests, and which requirement do they prove?
answer: The cool-off is gate 4.5 of requirement 8d's arming step: only at `agent-merges-all` and only for a pull request that touches a protected path, it refuses until `landing_cool_off_hours` (24 by default, `0` disables it) has passed since the `submitted_at` of the Approver's standing review, and a review `commit_id` that no longer matches the head (a push after approval) refuses however much time has passed. Acceptance check 8t pins it: `test/landing.test.sh` covers `landing_cool_off_effective_hours` (repository override, else top-level key, else 24), `landing_cool_off_remaining_hours` and `landing_protected_path_controls_ok` (which refuses naming the remaining time while the wait is open, refuses on a head mismatch even after a full day, and returns `ok` once the wait has elapsed or is `0`), while `test/landing-wiring.test.sh` shows the gate is never consulted below `agent-merges-all` and that its refusal arms nothing, and `test/doctor.test.sh` covers the doctor warning for `agent-merges-all` with a cool-off of `0`. Acceptance check 62 covers the refusal notice on the pull request: `_landing_notice_eligible_at` computes the eligible-at time as the approval time plus `landing_cool_off_hours`, and a changing countdown does not re-post the notice.

acceptance check 8t

question: What are the owner-only conditions that force an Enabler or Refiner escalation, where are they defined, and can any escalation_autonomy rung loosen them?
answer: They are "The owner-only boundary" in requirement 36a, written once there and referenced (never restated) by `prompts/enabler.md`, `prompts/enabler-decide.md` and `prompts/refiner.md`, and its nine conditions say a decision must escalate if it (1) spends money or changes a cap, budget, model tier or node count; (2) touches credentials, secrets, GitHub Apps, rulesets, permissions or account settings; (3) touches licence, revenue or pricing; (4) adds or changes a roadmap decision, phase gate or roadmap item; (5) creates an ongoing human obligation; (6) moves a trust boundary such as `merge_autonomy`, `escalation_autonomy`, the protected paths, a kill switch or the Approver's identity; (7) depends on an external service or account the pipeline does not hold; (8) needs information that exists only in someone's head; or (9) was reserved by its author with the `pw::owner-decision` label or an `Owner decision: yes` line, never by prose alone. Conditions 7 and 8 are narrowed by the host-facts carve-out when a node's host-facts record already carries the fact. No rung changes the list except requirement 36f's delegate mandate at `decide-with-veto`, which reaches only condition 2's acceptance clause and the human corroboration of a void for three pull-request shapes; acceptance check 36f proves that mandate (`test/escalation-autonomy.test.sh`, `test/enabler-verdicts.test.sh`, `test/decision-veto-sweep.test.sh`).

question: Which requirements say what a stage prompt must contain and how it is delivered to claude, and which tests prove each?
answer: Requirement 4c says every stage is run as `claude -p` with its assembled prompt on standard input (a here-string, so the exit status is the stage's own), never as a command-line argument, because Linux caps a single argv entry at `MAX_ARG_STRLEN` (131072 bytes); acceptance check 1k proves it with `test/stage-prompt-delivery.test.sh`, which sends a 200000-byte prompt through `run_claude_stage` (`lib/stage-run.sh`) and asserts it arrives whole on stdin and nowhere in argv. question: Where is the rule for what counts as a documentation-only change (one that builds no image) specified and tested, and does editing a prompts/*.md file count?

question: Which requirement governs the merge budget — what it counts and what happens at and past the cap — and which tests pin it?
answer: Requirement 2.3c governs it, implemented in `lib/merge-budget.sh` (component 14d): `merge_budget_per_day` (8 by default, overridable per `repos[]` entry, `0` meaning unlimited) caps how many of this pipeline's labelled pull requests one repository may land in a rolling 24 hours, counted from GitHub's own merged-PR record rather than a private counter. `merge_budget_decide` answers `arm`, `hold` (cap reached: the pull request is approved but its landing is not armed, so the backlog stays visible) or `refuse` (the count could not be read, failing closed), and it runs as gate 5 of requirement 8d's arming step; landing more than the cap is a counting anomaly that freezes that repository to `agent-approves` through `fleet/merge-budget-freeze-<slug>.json` and files an escalation in that repository. `test/merge-budget.test.sh` pins the decide and apply functions and `test/merge-autonomy.test.sh` pins the freeze's effect on `merge_autonomy_effective_level`; acceptance check 8t asserts that a `hold` or `refuse` arms nothing, and check 8u asserts that a shared ALREADY_ARMED tally keeps the retry sweep and the round's own arming within the remaining budget without reporting a false anomaly.

question: The Enabler's per-item claims are never released, which looks like a lock leak. Which design decision explains that, which requirements implement it, and which check proves the shortened retry?
answer: The Design decisions entry "The Enabler's claims are tombstones, not locks it releases" explains it: the failure being bounded is not two nodes racing but an engagement that leaves no record (a timeout, a garbage final message, an omitted item), and releasing the claim would let the next cycle re-engage the same unchanged item at Opus prices, cycle after cycle. Requirement 35c implements it: the per-item claim under the `enabler` pseudo-slug, keyed with the block's timestamp so that a re-blocked item gets a fresh key, is never released, and only `lib/claim.sh gc` sweeping it at `claim_ttl_hours` permits a retry, which bounds a failed engagement at one attempt per TTL. Requirement 37 shortens that wait for an engagement the Script watched fail even after the salvage resume: `lib/claim.sh expire` backdates the entry's `ts` so the next `gc` retires it, rather than releasing it. Acceptance check 11c proves it: a broken Enabler leaves the cycle's outcome unchanged, and `test/claim.test.sh` shows an expired entry still exists with its `ts` backdated and is retired by the next `gc` run.

question: My log is full of `stand-down` events whose reason begins `no-op short-circuit: no work source has changed since the Co-Ordinator found nothing to do at …`. Is the pipeline stuck, and how would I tell if it is actually missing work?
answer: No — on a quiet repository that is the system working. Before waking the Co-Ordinator, each cycle fingerprints everything the Co-Ordinator's verdict depends on (each repository's head commit, open issues with their labels, assignees and Priority, open pull requests, workflow conclusions, the blocked and void lists, the selection config and the prompt), and when that matches the fingerprint recorded at the last `none-selected` it stands down for the price of a few `gh` calls instead of paying for a run whose answer cannot have changed. It only ever claims "nothing changed", never "there is no work", and the `none_selected_recheck_hours` valve forces a Co-Ordinator run anyway once the last `none-selected` is old enough (24 cycle firings by default). It is a fault only if real work is waiting: run `./agent-cycle.sh --once`, which bypasses the short-circuit, and if that picks up work the scheduled cycles were skipping, the fingerprint is missing a signal and that is a bug worth filing.

`--once` bypasses the short-circuit and forces the Co-Ordinator to run

question: An issue I did not write has turned up in my repository, assigned to me and labelled `pw::enabler-escalation`. What is it asking for, and how am I supposed to answer it?
answer: It was raised by the Enabler — the occasional Opus pass that re-examines an item that has been blocked for several cycles — because it concluded that only a human can move that item, for example a secret only you can set, logs only you can see, or a decision that is yours to make. Do the thing it asks and then close the issue: closing is the whole protocol, with no reply, log edit or re-run expected (where it asks you a question, answer in a comment and then close it). The next cycle notices the closure, the Enabler re-checks the item against reality, and the work resumes or the thread gets a note saying what is still missing. It is assigned to you on purpose, because an assigned issue is excluded from the pipeline's own `issues` work source, so the pipeline can never pick up its own request for help as work.

it is assigned to you so the pipeline never selects its own request for help as work

question: The log shows `claim-lost` events — mostly with `cause: "held"`, a few with `"pr-held"`, and one burst with `"unreachable"`. Do any of these mean something is broken, and what does the cycle do after one?
answer: A `claim-lost` means the cycle tried to take the atomic, create-only claim on one of its ranked candidates and GitHub refused it, so the cycle moved on to the next-ranked candidate. `held` means another node already holds that item's claim — healthy contention, with the work being done elsewhere — and `pr-held` is the same healthy contention on the second, pull-request-keyed claim, meaning a peer is already working that pull request under a different item reference. `unreachable` means GitHub could not be reached at all, which is an outage rather than contention: nobody is doing that work. If every candidate is lost the cycle stands down — with cause `raced`, which chains another selection cycle, or, when every miss was `unreachable`, with a reason naming the outage, which does not chain.
must_mention: `held` means another node already holds the item's claim — healthy contention, not a fault
`pr-held` means a peer already holds the claim on the same pull request
`unreachable` means GitHub could not be reached — an outage, not contention
the cycle moves on to the next-ranked candidate, standing down only if every candidate is lost

question: A `limit-hit` event appeared with `class: "monthly"` and `reset_known: false`. What happens to cycles from now on, and do I have to do anything to get them running again?
answer: Every node in the fleet now stands down at the start of each cycle until `resume_at`, which is carried both in `fleet/limit.json` on the state repository and in the log (the later of the two wins). `reset_known: false` means the limit message stated no reset time, so `resume_at` is only this system's own estimated upper bound, not a real deadline. While the stand-down holds, each cycle probes the account with one minimal request and retires the stand-down by itself, logging `limit-cleared`, the moment the account answers. You can simply wait, or raise the cap and run `agent-cycle.sh --clear-limit "<reason>"` to bring the fleet back at once; `--enable` does not touch a usage-limit stand-down, because it is a separate state from the switch.
must_mention: the whole fleet stands down until `resume_at`
with `reset_known: false`, `resume_at` is only an estimated upper bound
each cycle probes the account and lifts the stand-down automatically (`limit-cleared`) once it answers
`--clear-limit` lifts it by hand after raising the cap; `--enable` does not

question: The dashboard's void list shows one of my items as void, with a reason saying the work is already done on `main`, but I am sure it has regressed. What does void mean, and how do I get the pipeline to look at it again?
answer: Void means the pipeline concluded there is no work — the item is already done or its premise was false — and, unlike a blocked item, which the pipeline re-checks and clears itself, a void is permanent: no agent can ever clear it. Only a human can reopen it, by applying the unvoid label (`pw::unvoided` by default, the `unvoid_label` setting) to any issue or pull request in that item's repository that names the item. The next cycle reads the label, reopens the void and puts the item back in the Co-Ordinator's pool in that same cycle; if there really is no work, the Implementer will simply void it again, with evidence. Leave the label where it is: it only reopens voids recorded before it was applied, so it cannot clear a fresh verdict later.

sources.heading: An item is blocked or void

must_mention: void means there is no work (already done, or a false premise) and no agent can ever clear it
apply the unvoid label (`pw::unvoided` by default) to an issue or pull request that names the item
the item is back in the Co-Ordinator's pool from the next cycle
the label only reopens voids recorded before it was applied, so it can be left in place

question: The pipeline has put `pw::needs-refinement`, `blocked` and `blocked:needs-refinement` on one of my issues. What is it telling me, and if I just take the labels off will it start work on the issue?
answer: The pipeline has recorded the issue as blocked because nobody has written down what the work actually is — no end state or acceptance criteria it could rank or implement — as reported by the Co-Ordinator, by a Refiner that declined to specify it, or by an Implementer that found the brief insufficient. The labels mirror that block so a filtered issue list shows it, and `blocked` keeps the issue off the pipeline's candidate list. Taking them off does nothing for a block the pipeline made, because those labels are a one-way projection of state the log holds; only a block you created yourself, by applying the needs-refinement label by hand, clears when you remove it. After a few cycles the Enabler either writes the specification as a comment on the issue (goal, scope, acceptance criteria, relevant files), which unblocks it and takes the label off, or asks you through a separate escalation issue that you answer in comments and then close.

sources.heading: An item is blocked or void

must_mention: the issue has no usable specification (end state or acceptance criteria), so the pipeline recorded it as blocked
removing the labels does nothing for a block the pipeline made; it only clears a block you created by applying the label yourself
the Enabler later writes a specification as a comment and removes the label, or asks you in a separate escalation issue

question: The pipeline left a comment on one of my pull requests saying it "has been approved, mergeable and green for over 24h with nothing further for the pipeline to do — … it is waiting on a merge click." Why did that appear, and is it going to keep posting these?
answer: It is the idle nudge from the human-visibility sweep that runs every cycle: the pull request is approved, mergeable, not blocked, has every check genuinely green, and has sat that way for longer than `human_nudge_idle_hours` (24 by default), so the only thing left is for you to merge it. It is posted once, not repeated — a hidden marker in the comment lets the sweep see that it has already nudged — and it is separate from the live review request the pipeline keeps re-asking on every ready pull request. It is never posted on a pull request you have already put in a GitHub merge queue, and setting `human_nudge_idle_hours` to `0` turns the nudge off.
must_mention: the pull request is approved, mergeable and green and has been idle longer than `human_nudge_idle_hours` (24 hours by default)
it is waiting only on a human to merge it
the nudge is posted once and not repeated
it is not posted on a pull request already in a merge queue

question: There is a closed, unassigned issue labelled `pw::decision` in my repository that I never opened. Is it asking me for something, and what can I do if I disagree with what it says?
answer: No — it is a durable log of a decision the pipeline took on its own authority (the Enabler's decision pass, at an `escalation_autonomy` of `decide-tactical` or `decide-with-veto`), carrying the decision, the rationale, the options considered and any act the decision carries with when that act becomes due; it is filed closed because it is a record, not an ask. To veto it, reopen it: the pipeline re-blocks the item, comments on it, flips any open pull request for it back to draft, and waits for your own decision, posted as a comment on the reopened issue, before you close it again. A reopen is honoured whenever it comes, and one that arrives before a pending act is due cancels the act outright. If the item has already merged or closed, there is nothing to re-block, so the pipeline files a fresh "revisit: …" issue quoting your comment instead.

sources.heading: An item is blocked or void

must_mention: it is a record of a decision the pipeline took itself, not a request
reopening the issue vetoes the decision
on a veto the pipeline re-blocks the item, flips any open pull request back to draft and waits for your decision as a comment on the issue
a reopen before a pending act is due cancels the act

question: The dashboard is showing a pager-firing banner with a badge on some node cards, and an issue labelled `pw::pager` has appeared. What filed it, do I have to do something, and will it go away on its own?
answer: The dashboard's Publisher filed it, not an implementation cycle: one of the fleet-level invariants it evaluates from the union fleet log and every peer's heartbeat has been firing continuously for `pager_min_firing_minutes` (15 by default), so it files one deduplicated `pw::pager` issue per invariant in `pager_repo` (falling back to `crash_loop_repo`), and the node-card badges mark the nodes the evidence names. Whether you must act depends on the invariant's remedy class: a `pipeline-act` invariant's fix is performed by the pipeline itself, a `config-lever` one also files a `pw::decision` record you can reopen to veto, and an `owner-only` one is assigned to you because only you can decide it. Once the invariant evaluates clear, the issue is closed automatically with a one-line comment saying the fact cleared.
must_mention: the dashboard Publisher filed it because a fleet-level invariant has been firing continuously for `pager_min_firing_minutes` (15 minutes by default)
there is one issue per firing invariant
owner-only invariants are assigned to you, while pipeline-act ones are fixed by the pipeline itself
it is closed automatically with a one-line comment once the fact clears
